articles.title: Turkey to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Turkey to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks  Middle East EyeTurkey sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say  ReutersWorld’s most powerful military and Africa avoids direct combat as Türkiye prepares to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia  Business Insider AfricaTurkey and Pakistan to send troops to support Saudi Arabia  The TimesTurkey prepares Saudi ...
articles.full_text:
Turkey plans to step up its military support for Saudi Arabia in the coming weeks by deploying additional personnel and defence equipment amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, several Turkish officials told Middle East Eye on Tuesday.
In a joint statement on Monday, Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia said they had decided to immediately implement their collective defence commitments under the Makkah Alliance for Defence and provide "the agreed military forces and capabilities to ensure their rapid deployment" to the kingdom.
Two Turkish officials familiar with Ankara's plans told MEE that Turkey had maintained technical teams, air defence systems and electronic warfare equipment in the kingdom since last year to protect critical infrastructure, including energy facilities.
One senior Turkish official said Ankara would send additional equipment, technicians, emergency response teams and accompanying combat forces.
The official said a 2010 military training agreement between Saudi Arabia and Turkey allows Ankara to deploy limited forces to the kingdom for technical purposes. Further deployments, however, would require parliamentary authorisation under the Turkish constitution.
"We have to ratify the Makkah treaty as well but we may prioritise the military deployment authorisation bill," the official added.
A second Turkish official said Ankara planned to station military forces at at least one command base, solely to provide defensive support to Saudi Arabia.
"Technical teams carried out work in Saudi Arabia throughout September for the command base project, and preparations were nearing completion around the time the first Makkah Strategic Political and Defence Committee meeting was held," the official said.
The officials said a limited number of Turkish special forces could be deployed to the kingdom after the Turkish parliament approves a formal authorisation, which is expected later this month.
Separate sources familiar with the planning told MEE that, following parliamentary approval, the Turkish military would deploy an undisclosed number of experienced pilots and aircraft to Saudi Arabia to counter drones and ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis in Yemen.
"We don't plan to send a large group of soldiers and have no plans to directly intervene in Yemen," the senior Turkish official said.
"Ankara still believes diplomatic efforts might bear fruit in coming months."
Protect Riyadh, holy sites and major pipeline
The Turkish military is expected to help protect the western section of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and contribute to the defence of Riyadh and the holy cities.
Saudi sources told MEE that Turkish forces would operate alongside their Saudi and Pakistani counterparts at a joint coordination base, while the Turkish command unit would maintain a separate base of its own.
Turkish military personnel and technical defence support teams would be responsible for operations across multiple locations.
Murat Yesiltas, an academic and a member of Turkish Presidency's advisory board on foreign policy, said that Ankara would likely bring the Mecca Pact, or a deployment authorisation, to the Turkish Grand National Assembly's agenda within the next 30 days.
"Turkey's initial contribution, however, is far more likely to take the form of air defense, anti-drone systems, or intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) elements on Saudi Arabian soil, rather than deploying combat troops in Yemen," he wrote in a social media post.
"This approach allows Turkey to integrate into Riyadh's security network while simultaneously enabling it to controllably limit the level of risk and engagement it undertakes."
MEE was first to report in September that Turkey was preparing to provide defensive assistance to the kingdom while avoiding direct intervention inside Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis have denied trying to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, with the group's leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, calling the claims last month a "major lie."

articles.title: Iran sends Hezbollah $200M for Lebanon war aid
articles.summary: Iran has provided Hezbollah with $200 million to support Lebanese families displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, marking...
articles.full_text:
Iran has provided Hezbollah with $200 million to support Lebanese families displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, marking the group’s first major aid effort for supporters hit hardest by the conflict.
Hezbollah received the funds last month despite mounting U.S. economic pressure on Iran and growing obstacles to moving money to Tehran’s Lebanese ally, the sources said.
Intermediaries handling the transfer charged a 20% fee because of the risks involved in dealing with Hezbollah, according to the sources. One said the rate was four times the usual fee.
A Hezbollah official, asked for comment, confirmed that funds had been secured and said a distribution plan would be announced in the coming days, but did not identify the source of the money.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry, its permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Treasury Department and the Lebanese government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel’s bombardment and ground offensive in Lebanon displaced hundreds of thousands of people, many from Hezbollah’s Shiite support base, after the Iran-backed group entered the regional conflict on March 2.
Hezbollah, founded with support from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has suffered heavy Israeli blows during two wars since 2024. The United States designates the group as a terrorist organization.
Many of those displaced have received little or no assistance from Hezbollah so far.
Hezbollah plans to use the funds to provide an initial $3,000 payment to each eligible family, with priority given to people whose villages have been destroyed or remain inaccessible because of Israeli occupation, the sources said.
About 50,000 families fall into those categories, according to one of the sources.
Iran has continued supporting Hezbollah despite years of U.S. sanctions. Tehran transferred $1 billion to the group during the first 10 months of 2025, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.
Tehran has not publicly acknowledged financing Hezbollah. Iran’s support for allied armed groups across the region has previously fueled domestic criticism, making the issue particularly sensitive as economic hardship deepens inside the country.
Iran had pledged additional funding for Hezbollah after Tehran reached an interim agreement with Washington in June that allowed it to sell oil. The agreement collapsed in July.
Washington has since intensified economic pressure on Tehran, tightening sanctions and imposing a naval blockade aimed at restricting Iranian oil exports.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said last month that the group would soon contribute to a project to house thousands of people displaced by the war, using “available resources and donations.” He did not provide further details.
Hezbollah’s ability to finance social services and postwar assistance has helped sustain support for the group in the past. After its 2006 war with Israel, Hezbollah quickly distributed cash to affected families and helped rebuild Beirut’s southern suburbs, one of its main strongholds.
This time, however, reconstruction has been slow. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that rebuilding after the two wars since 2024 could cost more than $27 billion.
The two sources did not disclose how the $200 million reached Lebanon.
One said Hezbollah was finding it increasingly difficult to transfer funds through financial companies that had previously handled such transactions. Firms in Iraq and Dubai were no longer viable options, while similar channels in Türkiye were also coming under pressure, the source said.
Hezbollah’s opponents increasingly view its access to money as crucial to the group’s ability to operate, the source added.
Despite the funding difficulties, Hezbollah has continued paying its fighters and providing money to the families of members killed in combat, according to the same source.
The conflict has exacted a heavy toll on Lebanon’s Shiite community, from which Hezbollah draws much of its support. Israel has destroyed villages across areas it seized in southern Lebanon, saying its operations are intended to protect northern Israel from Hezbollah attacks.
Israeli attacks in Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since March 2, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. The ministry does not distinguish between civilians and combatants in its toll.
Hezbollah has not disclosed how many of its fighters have been killed. Reuters reported on May 4 that several thousand Hezbollah fighters had died in the conflict.

articles.title: Yemen conflict escalates as Houthis hit Aden airport, target Riyadh
articles.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels targeted Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive drones early Wednesday, the Transport Ministry said, amid intensifying combat betwee...
articles.full_text:
Yemen's Houthi rebels targeted Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive drones early Wednesday, the Transport Ministry said, amid intensifying combat between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed forces.
The Saudi-led coalition, pushing to retake strategic territory seized by the Houthis, said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The escalation came after Yemeni government forces, with Saudi-led coalition air support, launched a lightning counteroffensive this week to capture the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait shipping route and the city of Mokha.
Yemen's government said that forced the Houthis out of areas they had captured last month, reviving a complex 12-year war, which led to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises and fragmented the Arab world's most impoverished country.
One missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control.
The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport.
The Houthis, which control much of Yemen's north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran's influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. A U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement, with a spillover from the Iran conflict triggering the latest fighting.
The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran's Middle East proxy network and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations.
Earlier Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. It was not immediately clear whether this was linked to the missile the coalition said it had intercepted near Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

UAE developer Arada has integrated Australian contractor Roberts into the UAE market as part of its wider business strategy.
Arada acquired Roberts in 2025 after entering the Australian market. The tier-one contractor delivers projects in the healthcare, education, commercial, residential, hospitality, industrial, life sciences and defence sectors.
At the time of the acquisition, Arada said it planned to invest about $20m in Roberts. The investment is intended to give the developer greater control over the delivery of its Australian projects and support Roberts’ expansion into markets including the UAE.
Arada has said it could invest up to $100m in Roberts’ expansion into new sectors and markets. The company is targeting $1bn in annual revenue from Roberts by 2028.
Roberts has established a UAE office, with a head office team already in place. Arada said the contractor’s capabilities will support the delivery of its high-rise residential and social infrastructure projects.
The contractor’s first UAE project will be phase two of Arada Central Business District, a commercial development within Aljada in Sharjah. Arada is developing the AED35bn ($9.5bn) mixed-use project.
Roberts is also providing preconstruction services for several Arada projects in Dubai and Sharjah, ahead of starting site work.

Large fires have broken out at a major oil pipeline and storage facility in Russia’s Samara Oblast, according to footage shared on social media and NASA satellite monitoring.
Footage posted to social media showed large fires and clouds of black smoke above the facility, which is a major node in Russia's network of oil pipelines.
NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which uses satellite data to detect thermal anomalies and fires, detected multiple hotspots at the facility.
The facility, which is located near the village of Prosvet, in Samara Oblast, includes pumping stations, tank farms, and blending stations. It has been a repeated target during Ukraine's campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil infrastructure.
Earlier that day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alluded to a Ukrainian strike on oil facilities in Samara Oblast, without specifying which facility had been hit.
While the cause of the current fire has yet to be officially stated, earlier on Oct. 7 Ukraine's General Staff confirmed damage caused to the facility in a previous Ukrainian drone strike on Oct. 2.
"As a result of the October 2, 2026 strike on the LVDS "Samara" in Prosveta, Samara Oblast of the Russian Federation, damage to eleven RVS-20000 tanks, three RVS-50000 tanks, sections of pipelines, and an automated oil production station was confirmed," the General Staff said in a statement.
The strikes on Russian oil infrastructure are aimed at "reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," they said.

The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said on Tuesday that it intercepted a missile fired by the group at the kingdom, which backs the pro-government forces that have launched a major operation to recapture lost territory.
The Iran-backed Houthis had earlier claimed an attack on the Saudi capital's main airport and on Tuesday denied being pushed back by government forces.

Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the coalition, said on X that it "intercepted and destroyed" a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, home to an airbase.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group still held all territory seized last month when they swept through coastal areas along the Red Sea, a vital global shipping route.
Houthi fighters "have full control over all their advances on the ground", he posted on Telegram.
Saree said they had carried out dozens of strikes in the past few hours targeting government forces in Yemen's Al-Jawf and Marib regions, while also attacking Taiz governorate.
He later said the Houthis had pushed back government forces "as they attempted to advance towards our forces' positions southwest of Al-Waziya", a strategic position to secure the Bab al-Mandab strait.
The Houthis' health ministry meanwhile said Tuesday that a Saudi airstrike killed six members of a family, including four children, in a village in Hajjah governorate.
On Monday, the Houthis said they had struck Riyadh airport and a refinery belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport is facing frequent temporary closures of its airspace, according to tracking website Flightradar24.
On Tuesday, the civil aviation authority said at least three people were wounded in attacks on Jazan and Najran airports near the Yemen border a day earlier.

Government forces claimed late on Monday that they had achieved "victories on several fronts".

They also said they expelled the Houthis from several areas in Taiz in the southwest, where fighting has surged in recent days.
Government forces also reported advances in the southern part of the governorate of Marib.
Yemen's government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory -- home to most of the country's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.

Hamish Kinnear, an analyst with UK-based Verisk Maplecroft, said the deployment "is likely to mean Turkey and Pakistan helping to intercept Houthi missiles and drones".

But "that distinction will become harder to maintain if the regional conflict continues to escalate".

articles.full_text:
Within the past month, the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have reignited a decades-long conflict.
At the heart of renewed fighting is control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key trading corridor better known as the Gate of Tears.
The Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast in September, seizing the port city of Mocha in a bid for power over the strait.
Now, Yemeni forces have recaptured the city in a major counteroffensive and deployed more than 100 fighter jets to guard the waterway.
But it is a fight that seems anywhere but over.
And one that could impact Australia's supply of everything, from T-shirts to medicine.
What is the Gate of Tears?
The Gate of Tears, or Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is a waterway at the southern end of the Red Sea — between Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea.
Named for its precarious route, it lies on the opposite side of the peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz, the shipping corridor whose traffic has been dramatically affected as the US and Iran wrestle for its control.
The strait is 29 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, limiting traffic to two channels for inbound and outbound shipments.
The Yemeni island of Perim divides the path.
To the north lie the port cities of Hodeidah and Mocha.The cities, which the Houthis have seized, give a commanding view over approaching vessels.
On September 11, the group also seized the strategic Perim, where the United Arab Emirates — a former Saudi ally — had been building an air base.
Since then, a Saudi-backed counteroffensive has regained control of Mocha and attacked Houthi members in Hodeidah.
What is behind this latest conflict?
The Houthis' desire to control the strait extends beyond the Iran war.
The fight over key ports are part of a continuing civil war in Yemen, between the Houthis and a Saudi-backed government.
From 2015 to the 2022 truce, Saudi Arabia was involved in a combined air and limited ground campaign in Yemen, fighting against the Houthis, a group Australia lists as a terrorist organisation.
The fragile truce collapsed this year, after an air strike hit the Sana'a International Airport, preventing an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation to land.
Houthis blamed the attack on a Saudi-led coalition, and responded with missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh.
They also targeted Saudi's oil infrastructure.
In July, the Houthis launched a maritime blockade on Saudi shipping tankers and territory in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The group had conducted a similar attack on commercial ships passing through the strait in 2023—2024, in response to Israel's invasion of the Gaza Strip.
However, this latest blockade exempted non-Saudi vessels.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, told the Associated Press it wanted Saudi Arabia to lift a long-running blockade on the territory the group controls.
A Saudi counteroffensive has since seen the strait recaptured and tit-for-tat fighting escalate.
Both Saudi and Houthi officials have reported missile strikes and targeted attacks on major airports across Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
The renewed conflict has also seen more than 200,000 Yemenis flee their homes, according to UN estimates.
The United Nations estimated at least 150,000 people — including fighters and civilians — had been killed in Yemen's civil war, which began in 2015.
It had pushed about 5 million people to the "brink of famine".
How important is Bab el-Mandeb to trade?
It serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal, meaning ships must pass through it to access the canal from the south.
Before the Iran war in February, about 10-12 per cent of global trade passed through the waterway, Sanjoy Paul, an associate professor of operations and supply chain management at the University of Technology Sydney said.
"It has always been a critical route for shipping," he added.
"It's not for only for few countries. Continents are connected through that shipping route."
In 2023, the strait handled approximately 9 per cent of global oil demand, according to the International Sustainable Development Observatory (ISDO).
And for Asia and Australia, the shipping lane is even more significant.
Oil, medicine, fertiliser, textiles, and machinery were all transported through that route, Dr Paul said.
When it was a choke point, ships had to travel around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope which could take three times as long.
"This additional time increases shipping time, increases cost of transportation, increases insurance as well," Dr Paul said.
For customers, that meant shortages and price surges.
Following the Iran war and a battle over the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait became a "lifeline", Dr Paul said.
Saudi Arabia had built an East-West Pipeline to divert crude oil flows through the Red Sea path
As of June, 3.42 million barrels of Saudi oil flowed through the strait, according to Kpler data.
"This became the alternative route," Dr Paul said.
What does this mean for Australia?
US President Donald Trump has been hesitant so far to become involved in this latest conflict, saying the Houthis "don't want to fight with us".
"They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through," he told reporters in late September.
But Qatar has warned the world cannot "afford" for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to close.
"The whole world is going to suffer and it's going to be catastrophic for the entire world," Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman, said.
Saudi Arabia exports about 70 per-cent of the global oil supply, and most of its buyers are Asian nations who sell onto Australia.
If the fight for control was to escalate, it might lead to a particularly "devastating impact" on Australia's oil supply, Dr Paul said.
He said a further blockade would be "another blow to shipping and transportation", in addition to decreased use of the Strait of Hormuz.
"That increased demand at a global level will again translate into higher prices," Dr Paul added, about the impact on Australian fuel.
While a chokehold may hit consumer pockets, Dr Paul was concerned about Australia's access to critical supplies, such as medicine.
"It could be another important consideration: How in Australia we can prepare to stock key medicine?" Dr Paul said.
"Because those sort of things will be impacted for a long time.
"We may need to rethink our medical situation, how we can have enough stock here.
"How long can you rely on those countries that cannot bring in your products?"

articles.summary: Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says  Al JazeeraAttacks on Saudi airports kill three people, as fighting escalates in Yemen  ReutersDeadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports highlight widening fallout from Yemen civil war  CNN3 Killed and Dozens Injured in Attacks on Saudi Airports, as Houthis Claim Strikes  The New York TimesHouthi rebels target Riyadh and Aden in new missile barrage  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, GACA reported.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.
GACA said it is working “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities” to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
Previous attacks on Saudi airports
New cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport.
On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swathe of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones against Aden airport early on Wednesday. No casualties were reported.
Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

articles.title: Israeli campaign to erase Gaza towns exposed by satellite images
articles.summary: Satellite imagery has exposed how the Israeli military has systematically erased the city of Rafah, once home to 250,000 people, as part of its three-year genocidal war in the Gaza...
articles.full_text:
Satellite imagery has exposed how the Israeli military has systematically erased the city of Rafah, once home to 250,000 people, as part of its three-year genocidal war in the Gaza Strip.
Demolition, using bulldozers and explosives, has continued unabated since the Israel-Hamas cease-fire deal reached a year ago, as the military solidifies its hold on just over 60% of the territory that it still controls.
Gaza's mangled landscape is just one of the wounds on top of wounds that the enclave's 2 million Palestinians have endured since Israel launched its genocidal war after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion on southern Israel.
More than one out of every 10 people from Gaza's prewar population has been killed or wounded by Israeli fire. While nearly every family mourns dead or cares for wounded, most also had to move multiple times to escape fighting and Israeli evacuation orders. With almost the entire population homeless, the coastal territory is now effectively one of the world's most populated tent cities. Ramshackle canvas and nylon shelters blanket beaches and former agricultural lands and fill empty lots.
Little is likely to change for the foreseeable future. While the cease-fire deal stopped the offensives and heaviest bombardment, Israel hits tents, cars and buildings almost daily in strikes that it says target Hamas members – but that regularly kill women, children and other family members.
People no longer have to flee from place to place, but few can rebuild homes because Israel bars most construction material from entering Gaza. The cease-fire agreement's plan for the large-scale reconstruction of Gaza has never gotten off the ground because of a Israeli stranglehold and Hamas' proposal of a gradual disarmament.
Najwa Abu Eita lost her 7-year-old daughter when Israeli forces struck her home in the central refugee camp of Nuseirat in September 2024, and her three other children were injured in the attack. Abu Eita lost an eye, her face remains heavily damaged and scarred, and she has trouble breathing.
A hairdresser before the war, she now has no work, living in a tent by the ruins of her home. Worst of all, she says, her children are frightened by her face and avoid looking at her.
"My 4-year-old son tells me, 'Momma, I'll give you one of my eyes.' And inside, I'm weeping," she said.
Gaza's population is squeezed into about 40% of the tiny territory, and Israel's military controls the rest. Satellite imagery by Planet Labs PBC shows that the vast majority of buildings in the Israel-held part have been bulldozed or exploded down to piles of rubble, much of it after major fighting ended a year ago.
The Israeli military says it demolishes buildings to prevent their use by Hamas members or to destroy the group's tunnel networks.
But a U.N.-appointed expert said in a February report that the scale of destruction of civilian housing and infrastructure in Gaza "is unprecedented even by the terrible standards of modern warfare since the 20th century."
The report warned that it could constitute a crime against humanity or reach the level of genocide, which under international law includes "deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction."
Israel rejects accusations of genocide, saying it targets Hamas militants and their infrastructure that are interwoven with civilian areas.
The Planet Labs imagery shows at least 50 Israeli military outposts built throughout the Israeli-held part of Gaza, at least 18 of them constructed since the cease-fire began. Many have been put on top of former neighborhoods where the rubble of demolished buildings nearby has been cleared away.
Most of Rafah was razed before the cease-fire, but images show that troops continue to demolish the few remaining buildings. Several abandoned U.N. buildings have been spared, as well as a municipal sports field that now appears to contain a military base.
A new base also stands on what was once the main intersection of the southern town of Bani Suheila. Leveled over the past year, the town is now a wasteland intersected by a spiderweb of dirt paths that were once streets.
In Jabaliya in the north, most of the al-Awda Hospital Complex was reduced to rubble in recent months, as were a number of U.N.-run school buildings, satellite images show. Jabaliya was once home to the Gaza Strip's biggest refugee camp, home to some 120,000 refugees and tens of thousands of other residents in a densely built urban district.
Now one of the few buildings still standing is the octagonal-shaped Indonesian Hospital, empty since troops shut it down in June 2025. The Israeli military built a new base nearby.
Similarly, most of Beit Hanoun, once a town of some 70,000 people in Gaza's far northeast corner, and Shijaiya, a Gaza City neighborhood founded 800 years ago, are now block after block of leveled houses and apartment towers.
An increased flow of aid and commercial products brought Gaza back from famine that arose in some areas last year under a monthslong Israeli ban on food and other goods. But most of the population remains dependent on international relief. Jobs are few, mostly connected to selling in the market.
Shadi Barawi lost his father early in the war. Soon after that, Barawi was hit by shrapnel from a strike near his home in Gaza City, and his leg was amputated – one of some 6,000 amputees left by the war.
After losing his leg, "I lost all hope in life," the 35-year-old said. But he was the sole support, he said, for his own family of six and his five sisters.
A barber before the war, he returned to giving haircuts to earn some money. With no prosthetic limb, he balances on his crutches as he works in the same tent where he lives.
"I'm working in tough circumstances," he said. "I'm on one leg. I might do cuts for three customers, then I get tired and stop and rest, but then I keep going," he said.
Thousands of bodies remain buried under buildings smashed by Israeli strikes. Since the cease-fire, Gaza authorities have slowly been going from site to site to try to find them.
Last week, a search team finally came to the Gaza City home of Haneen al-Khodari. When her building was hit in December 2023, al-Khodari was thrown into a nearby tree, and after weeks in the hospital, she was told her parents, siblings and many of her cousins were killed, she said. The bodies of 17 of them remained trapped under wreckage ever since.
But after eight hours digging through the ruins, the team only recovered the remains of a small child and two bones. The search for the rest was called off.
Al-Khodari sat on the pavement, her hopes dashed. "We had been waiting for this moment for three years," she said.
A plastic sheet on the ground in front of her contained what they'd found, labeled with the words, "Mixed bones."

articles.summary: Open Letter From 78 Military Professionals Rejecting Genocide Allegation Against Israel  JINSAOver 75 retired US military leaders reject Gaza genocide allegations in open letter  The Times of Israel“Origins of a Genocide”: Al Jazeera’s Marwan Bishara on “Twelve Days That Shook the Middle East”  Democracy Now!The Genocide Case Against Hamas  Jewish JournalZionism, apartheid and genocide: The argument the world can no longer avoid  Middle East Moni...
articles.full_text:
For Immediate Release
October 7, 2026
Washington, DC – As retired senior military leaders and legal experts, on this, the third anniversary of Hamas’s October 7, 2023 brutal attack on Israel, we reject claims that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Genocide is a grave and exceptional violation of international law, defined and prohibited by the Genocide Convention of 1948 and enumerated as a crime in the Statute of the International Criminal Court and in the U.S. federal criminal code. The allegations that Israel committed this crime do not meet the established definition and standards of genocide, are unsupported by established facts, nor do they stand up to common sense scrutiny.
A finding of genocide requires evidence of acts that are intended to destroy a protected national, ethnic, racial, or religious group, in whole or in part. Israel has neither intended to, nor destroyed, Palestinians as a group in Gaza. All the evidence, in fact, points to the contrary conclusion: that, after suffering a barbaric, indiscriminate massacre by Hamas terrorists on October 7, 2023, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), acting in justified self-defense, went to extreme lengths to protect civilians in Gaza, including from Hamas.
Israel’s accusers allege genocide mostly because of the supposed number of civilians killed in Gaza. Such claims are rife with flaws. Genocide is not a quantitative crime; there is no number of civilian casualties that constitutes genocide. Nor are the claimed casualty numbers from Gaza credible. Issued by Hamas themselves and, at the very least, not distinguishing between civilians and combatants, they cannot be relied upon.
Further, established legal precedent makes clear that civilian deaths occurring during combat, however tragic, are insufficient, by themselves, to support a finding of genocidal intent. That is because of the unfortunate realities of war and the laws that govern it, both of which Israel’s accusers appear woefully ignorant.
Many of the signatories to this letter have commanded United States armed forces in combat against enemies who regularly hide behind civilians and put those civilians intentionally in harm’s way. Fighting under those complexities is especially difficult. We understand that the loss of civilian life in Gaza is tragic. But we also know that such tragic outcomes do not necessarily violate the law of armed conflict. There is no perfect attack; there are only those in which commanders use all available information to make hard decisions and their best judgement to comply with legal obligations and protect civilians. And that is exactly what we have witnessed from the IDF in Gaza.
Assessments of Israeli combat operations, undertaken by some of the signatories to this letter, describe a military taking an unprecedented combination of precautions to avoid civilian casualties; not one following orders to destroy Palestinians as a group. The IDF has provided civilians with numerous advance warnings—leaflets, phone calls, text messages, radio and TV broadcasts, and social media notices—evacuation instructions, protected corridors, and tactical pauses to help move them out of harm’s way, even when those precautionary measures ceded tactical advantage to enemy forces. IDF soldiers have even put themselves in harm’s way to protect Palestinians seeking to flee the fighting from attack by Hamas. Stringent legal review of targets is a standard part of IDF procedures. Repeatedly, Israel has called off strikes because of the presence of civilians.
Israel has also gone out of its way to provide aid and assistance to civilians in Gaza. More than 3.5 million tons of food, 48,000 tons of medical supplies, 5,000 tons of baby food, and up to 15,000 cubic meters per day of water desalinated by Israel have been sent into Gaza. Over half a million Gazan children were vaccinated during the war and some 5,000 Gazans evacuated for medical treatment abroad. These are not the actions of a genocidal state but of a professional military ethically and legally committed to the protection of civilian life.
This pattern of law-abiding IDF conduct in Gaza also contradicts accusers’ claims that some statements from Israeli political officials, seemingly encouraging unlawful harm to civilians, are evidence of genocidal intent. Such inflammatory statements are disgraceful. Yet, while it deserves unequivocal condemnation, rhetoric from politicians uninvolved in military decision-making is in no way reflective of actual IDF operations.
Israel has not committed genocide but rather set a high bar for how to conduct urban warfare against an enemy who will stop at nothing, including the death of its own civilians.
We call on those concerned with this issue to carefully assess the facts related to the Gaza campaign, insist on faithful application of the Genocide Convention, and reject factually and legally dubious accusations against Israel. Failure to do so incentivizes future adversaries to deliberately endanger civilians and then exploit civilian suffering to portray lawful operations as genocide, weaken public support, and divide our alliances.
The precedent established today regarding Israel will shape the conditions under which American forces fight tomorrow. Protecting civilians and preserving the ability of our nation to defend itself requires us to defend the truth when the laws of war are being distorted to make false charges of genocide.

Dubai investors target Türkiye logistics as Gulf ties deepen
Dubai-based investors are scaling up capital commitments to Türkiye's logistics and rail sectors as the 2023 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement drives deeper economic integration between the UAE and Ankara, with officials highlighting the strategic importance of the Middle Corridor for Gulf-Europe trade.
Dubai-based investors are scaling up capital commitments to Türkiye's logistics and rail infrastructure as economic ties with the United Arab Emirates deepen following the 2023 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, according to officials familiar with the discussions. The strategic positioning of Türkiye between Europe and the Middle East has drawn particular interest from Emirati firms seeking to diversify trade routes through the Middle Corridor.
Deepening economic ties
Turkish companies continue to expand their presence in Gulf markets while Emirati capital flows into construction, real estate, food and healthcare sectors across Türkiye. The bilateral trade volume and cross-border investments have gained momentum since the Comprehensive Economic Partnership deal came into force last year, establishing a framework for mutual economic cooperation. Strengthening road and rail connections alongside port development remains central to these diversification efforts.
Strategic transport corridors
Mert Danisger, chief representative of the Dubai International Chamber's Türkiye Office, told Anadolu that recent regional developments have elevated the strategic importance of the Middle Corridor and the urgent need for alternative transport routes. "New railway projects connecting the Gulf to Türkiye will create a new logistics route, and once these infrastructure projects are implemented, we will ensure that goods are distributed from the Gulf to Europe via Türkiye more quickly and safely, while access to the Gulf region for European goods will become easier," he said. Danisger noted that such infrastructure would establish faster distribution channels while ensuring safer access for European goods entering Gulf markets.
Chamber cooperation initiatives
Turkish firms maintain strong participation at international trade fairs hosted in Dubai, with the Dubai Chambers working to facilitate market entry and cross-border investments. Danisger stated that the UAE represents a key economic partner for Ankara, with mutual trade and investments supporting cooperation across multiple sectors. The Türkiye Office continues to assist Turkish companies in penetrating the Gulf market while helping Emirati investors navigate opportunities in Turkish logistics and transport infrastructure.

articles.title: Beyond tariffs: The US–Turkey trade relationship needs a bigger bargain - Atlantic Council
articles.summary: Beyond tariffs: The US–Turkey trade relationship needs a bigger bargain  Atlantic Council
articles.full_text:
Turkey has much of what the United States wants from an economic-security partner, combining a strong manufacturing base with strategic geography and regional influence. Yet it faces a comparatively high tariff burden, and new risks stemming from its energy relationships with Russia and Iran.
The tension reflects a broader change in how Washington is using tariffs: not only to protect domestic industries, but to encourage trading partners to invest in the United States, align with US regulatory and economic-security priorities, and build more secure supply chains. The result is a trade system in which market access increasingly depends on a country’s contribution to US industrial and economic-security goals.
For Ankara, that means thinking beyond tariff relief. For Washingon, Turkey’s industrial capacity, strategic location, and access to important regional markets create the opportunity to turn a difficult trade relationship into an economic security partnership. A structured bargain linking tariff relief to greater bilateral trade, investment, and supply-chain security could advance the two countries’ longstanding $100 billion trade goal while deepening cooperation in strategically important sectors.
The evolution of US trade policy toward Turkey
During President Donald Trump’s first term, Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum, Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods, and the renegotiation of the North American Free Trade Agreement into the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement laid the foundation for an America First trade policy that, by the start of Trump’s second term, had evolved into a more integrated strategy linking trade policy with national security.
Turkey entered this environment through Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. In 2018, Turkish steel initially faced a 50 percent rate before reverting to 25 percent in 2019. In 2025, the United States expanded Section 232 coverage and raised the general steel and aluminum tariff rate to 50 percent before further restructuring the metals regime in 2026. Turkey exports more than $1 billion of steel annually to the United States, making steel a major source of friction.
Washington has since broadened both the legal authorities it uses and the objectives tariffs are intended to serve. In April 2025, a 10 percent tariff was imposed on Turkey as part of the initial “Liberation Day” tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), then the lowest rate applied to any major US trade partner. After the US Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, the White House imposed a temporary 10 percent import surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration then turned to a broader use of Section 301 of the Trade Act.
In July, the US Trade Representative (USTR) finalized tariffs under its forced-labor investigations covering sixty economies, including Turkey, for not having imposed and effectively enforced strong enough prohibitions on goods produced with forced labor. Economies that adopted, or committed to adopt, qualifying controls received a 10 percent rate. Turkey and most other investigated economies received a 12.5 percent rate. Notably, Turkey was not among the sixteen economies potentially subject to additional tariffs under a second Section 301 investigation into structural industrial excess capacity.
Turkey’s strategic value and economic security exposure
Several major US trade partners, including Japan, the European Union, South Korea, and Switzerland, have negotiated arrangements that cap their combined most-favored-nation and forced-labor Section 301 tariff burden at 10 percent or 12.5 percent. Turkey has no comparable arrangement.
Exposure also varies by product. Goods already covered by Section 232 are generally excluded from the forced-labor Section 301 tariffs, while products outside the Section 232 regime may instead fall under the new Section 301 tariffs. Ordinary customs duties and, for certain products, antidumping or countervailing duties can raise the final cost even further.
Furthermore, Turkey’s exposure increasingly extends beyond traditional tariff policy. The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 allows for tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports from certain major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, potentially including Turkey, in addition to other applicable tariffs.
Iran poses an additional challenge because Turkey has historically balanced its strong commercial and energy connections with Iran against US sanctions. On September 4, the Treasury Department sanctioned a Turkish financial institution and two affiliates, accusing them of helping Iran evade sanctions and manage oil revenue.
At the same time, Turkey’s industrial base and geography give it potential value to US economic security objectives. Its economy spans automotive production, machinery, aerospace and defense, steel, energy equipment, and advanced manufacturing, while its integration into European value chains gives Turkish firms experience in sophisticated production networks. Its location also provides commercial connectivity across the Black Sea, the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa, positioning it as a potential partner in US efforts to diversify strategic supply chains and reduce dependencies.
That potential spans across sectors vital to Washington’s economic security agenda. Turkey could contribute in areas such as critical minerals, energy, defense, advanced manufacturing, infrastructure, and regional logistics. Closer economic ties would not eliminate Turkey’s strategic independence or ensure alignment with US policies, but they could deepen cooperation on shared priorities, including energy and trade routes, infrastructure, and regional economic projects.
The opportunity for a broader US–Turkey bargain
In 2025, US–Turkey goods trade reached about $36.8 billion, including a roughly $4 billion US surplus in 2025. Overall trade in goods and services has more than doubled since 2019, when Trump and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan established a target of $100 billion in bilateral trade, but remains well short of that ambition.
Turkey has no reciprocal trade agreement that offers a clear path toward preferential tariff treatment or deeper economic cooperation. For Ankara, tariff relief should therefore form part of a broader negotiating agenda. Turkey could offer greater market access for US companies, address longstanding trade tensions, strengthen customs and supply-chain enforcement, and deepen regulatory cooperation in exchange for more predictable tariff treatment. An interim trade arrangement, potentially drawing on elements of US agreements with Taiwan and Indonesia, could provide a framework for addressing these issues while building toward a deeper economic relationship.
Turkey’s Digital Services Tax (DST) illustrates the potential bargaining space. USTR previously found the tax discriminatory and burdensome to US commerce, but Turkey later agreed to remove it once the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development Pillar One framework entered into force, prompting USTR to terminate its planned retaliatory tariffs. With that process unresolved, Turkey has instead begun phasing down the tax, from 7.5 percent to 5 percent in 2026 and 2.5 percent in 2027.
Addressing the DST would not directly affect Turkey’s 12.5 percent forced-labor tariff, but could remove a source of friction in broader negotiations. USTR’s July 2026 Section 301 action against Brazil shows that digital trade concerns remain part of Washington’s reciprocal trade and enforcement agenda.
Washington, in turn, should consider what it can offer. Tariff accommodations (including on Section 232 steel tariffs) along with improved market access and targeted US financing and investment could draw Turkey more deeply into trusted US supply chains while encouraging domestic and allied sourcing.
The administration has already shown willingness to calibrate tariffs where they could undermine broader economic security objectives, including through exclusions for selected raw materials and domestically unavailable inputs. Targeted accommodations could similarly support US industrial and supply-chain objectives.
Turkey’s comparative advantage in such a bargain would not be in matching the scale of US investment pledges made by Japan or South Korea. It would be its industrial capacity, geographic reach, and ability to support diversification across strategically important regions.
Steel offers an obvious place to test that proposition, but any accommodation would also require confronting global excess capacity and transshipment risks. Turkey’s participation in the September 2026 Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity provides a potential foundation for addressing those concerns alongside the United States and other major steel-producing economies.
Any deeper economic partnership could therefore be reciprocal, though not symmetrical. Turkey can offer greater market access, regulatory cooperation, supply-chain safeguards, sourcing transparency, and access to industrial and regional networks. The United States can offer capital, technology, financing, strategic investment, and potentially more favorable tariff treatment.
A structured US–Turkey economic security partnership could bring these elements together and provide a more concrete framework for their shared trade ambitions while lowering economic frictions, enhancing Turkey’s integration into US and allied supply chains, and reinforcing shared interests across strategically important regions.

articles.title: Oman and Kazakhstan Advance Indian Ocean Trade Corridor and Settle Dunga Oil Dispute - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Oman and Kazakhstan Advance Indian Ocean Trade Corridor and Settle Dunga Oil Dispute  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Oman and Kazakhstan have committed to developing a multimodal trade corridor connecting Central Asia to the Indian Ocean, anchoring a suite of economic agreements signed during the first-ever visit by an Omani monarch to Astana.
A New Logistics Architecture
Kazakhstan, the world's largest landlocked country, has historically relied on northern transit routes through the Russian Federation. Following the geopolitical shifts of recent years, Astana has aggressively sought alternative pathways to global markets. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said used the latter's historic state visit on Tuesday to formalize plans for a southern exit strategy.
The proposed corridor would leverage Kazakhstan's existing road and rail networks, linking them across the Caspian Sea or through intermediary states to Oman's deep-water ports. Sultan Haitham emphasized that Oman provides direct maritime access to the Gulf, the Indian Ocean, and East Africa, offering a complementary geographic advantage to Kazakhstan's position bridging Europe and Asia.
The initiative dovetails with Kazakhstan's ongoing development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, known as the Middle Corridor, and its participation in the CASA railway project traversing Afghanistan to Pakistan. While specific cargo volumes, transit tariffs, and physical infrastructure requirements remain undefined, the diplomatic commitment signals a concerted effort to physically integrate Central Asian resource markets with Gulf maritime hubs.
Resolving the Dunga Oil Field Deadlock
The most immediate commercial breakthrough of the summit was the resolution of a protracted dispute over the Dunga oil field, located in Kazakhstan's western Mangystau region. The asset is operated under a production-sharing agreement by Dunga Operating GmbH, which is 60 percent owned by Kazakhstan's state energy firm KazMunayGas, with Oman Oil Company Limited and Thailand's PTTEP each holding a 20 percent stake.
The disagreement centered on capital and operating expenses accumulated during previous phases of extraction, which the Kazakh government had classified as non-recoverable costs under the terms of the consortium's contract. On Monday, the Kazakh Energy Ministry and KazMunayGas signed a settlement agreement resolving these financial discrepancies. The documents will now be transmitted to the Omani and Thai partners for final signature.
The settlement unlocks a new development plan for the Dunga field extending from 2026 to 2039. The operational roadmap projects the extraction of 67.4 million barrels of oil over the 13-year period, supported by renewed capital investment that had been stalled by the cost-recovery dispute. This resolution removes a significant impediment to bilateral investment and demonstrates Astana's willingness to negotiate terms with long-standing Gulf partners.
Historical Foundations and Middle Power Diplomacy
The diplomatic relationship between Oman and Kazakhstan dates back to the immediate aftermath of the Soviet Union's dissolution. Oman was among the first Arab nations to formally recognize Kazakhstan's independence and was an early participant in the consortium established to transport oil from the massive Tengiz field. Despite this early engagement, trade volumes have historically remained modest, reaching approximately 22.9 million Omani rials (roughly $59 million) in the first half of 2026, up from minimal levels in 2025.
The current diplomatic push, spearheaded by Sultan Haitham, represents a deliberate strategy to transition the relationship from political goodwill to structural economic integration. Kazakhstan's foreign policy relies heavily on multi-vector diplomacy, seeking balanced relationships with global superpowers and regional anchors alike. Oman, maintaining its traditional role as a neutral mediator and pragmatic commercial actor in the Middle East, offers Astana an unencumbered gateway to Southern Hemisphere markets.
For the Omani delegation, Kazakhstan presents vast agricultural potential and critical mineral resources that align with Muscat's long-term food security and industrial diversification goals. The establishment of the joint investment fund is explicitly designed to channel Omani sovereign wealth into Kazakh infrastructure, ensuring that the proposed transport corridors have the financial backing necessary to move from concept to physical reality.
Expanding Bilateral Investment
Beyond logistics and hydrocarbons, the two governments executed five formal agreements and ten memoranda of understanding to institutionalize their economic relationship. The summit, which precedes the 35th anniversary of diplomatic ties between the two nations next year, established a joint investment fund and an Oman-Kazakhstan Business Council.
The agreements provide a framework for mutual investment protection and outline cooperation in emerging sectors, including artificial intelligence, digital technologies, and agriculture. Omani capital is already present in Kazakhstan's mining and gold industries, and the new frameworks aim to lower regulatory barriers for sovereign wealth and private sector engagement.
To support the anticipated increase in commercial exchange, the two sides agreed to expand direct air connectivity, a necessary precursor to developing tourism and streamlining executive travel between the two regions.
Strategic Implications
The alignment between Muscat and Astana reflects a broader recalibration of middle powers in the global economy. By securing a reliable partner in the Arab world, Kazakhstan mitigates the logistical vulnerabilities inherent in its geography. For Oman, integrating Kazakh commodities into its port infrastructure reinforces its status as a premier logistics hub outside the congested chokepoints of the upper Persian Gulf. By resolving legacy energy disputes and committing to integrated logistics, the two nations are attempting to engineer a resilient economic axis capable of withstanding regional volatility.

articles.title: US Vice President Vance ties ending war to Iran cutting enrichment
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance has said that Iran must "meaningfully" reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the seven-month war, though he noted Washington remains uncertain how T...
articles.full_text:
Vice President JD Vance has said that Iran must "meaningfully" reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the seven-month war, though he noted Washington remains uncertain how Tehran reaches negotiating decisions.
Vance, a longtime skeptic of U.S. involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in June that quickly fell apart.
The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.
Speaking to Reuters after a campaign trip in Alaska Monday, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said.
"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
Iran and the U.S. have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer and has warned that military operations could intensify after the midterms.
Vance said the U.S. remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions.
"We're not going to trade words for actions," Vance said.
Complicating matters, Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran.
Vance said the U.S. was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran's power structure, he said, after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed then Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his "biggest problem" is no one knows who is running Iran.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Sunday that U.S. officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran's decision-making system works.
"The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from U.S. officials," Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference.
Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions. He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway.
Vance declined to say if he was leading peace talks, though he is frequently cited as the White House's top negotiator.
"We're certainly involved," he said. "Ultimately, the president of the United States is driving things."
The war – and its $3 billion monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Vance has sought to temper criticism of Trump’s handling of the conflict, telling voters they should not let that issue keep them from backing Republicans in next month's elections.
In Alaska, Vance rallied for Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight reelection battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Trump carried Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but rising everyday costs have put the state in play.
Before speaking with Reuters, Vance focused much of his speech on affordability concerns, especially around energy. Alaska's remote locale makes consumer goods more expensive, and energy production is a key industry.
Rally attendees roared when Sullivan nearly introduced Vance as the president of the U.S., rather than the vice president. Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House.
Vance told Reuters afterward that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028.
"I'm inherently a procrastinator," he said. "I really haven't thought about it much."

articles.summary: Palestinian killed, 16 wounded in Israeli pogrom in occupied West Bank  Al JazeeraIsraeli settlers beat AFP photographer covering violence in West Bank  The Washington PostResidents of West Bank’s last Christian village ‘living in fear’  Vatican NewsIDF Threatens to Close Palestinian Olive Groves if Activists Accompany Farmers  HaaretzSettler violence is disrupting the Palestinian olive harvest  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
A Palestinian has been killed and 16 others wounded in a pogrom by settlers under the protection of Israeli forces in the northern occupied West Bank, Palestinian authorities said.
Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, from Burqa, northwest of Nablus, was killed in the attack on Palestinians harvesting olives on farmland near Burqa, west of Nablus, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.
Several of those wounded, including a woman, were taken to hospitals in Tulkarem and Nablus, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported, citing local sources.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) said its teams treated five people in the area, including two who suffered gunshot wounds, while the other three were beaten, Wafa reported.
PRCS said Israeli forces also assaulted ambulance crews trying to reach the injured people, and briefly detained three paramedics and a volunteer.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks, describing them as “war crimes”.
In a statement, the ministry urged the international community to fulfill its “legal and moral responsibilities” and provide international protection for Palestinians.
Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim, reporting from Ramallah, said the violence comes amid escalating attacks on Palestinians during the olive harvest season.
“If you just go to pick your olives now … you could not return from the journey. It could be dangerous, not only because of Israeli restrictions against farmers going to their lands, but also because of the armed Israeli settlers who continue to assault Palestinians,” Ibrahim said.
She said the attacks have transformed an important social and economic season for Palestinian families.
“In October, usually Palestinians take days off from their jobs and go to the land, try and pick their olives because this is supposed to be a joyous season,” she added.
Israeli forces and settlers also assaulted several Palestinians harvesting olives near Anata in the central occupied West Bank, Wafa reported.
Elsewhere, settlers cut down at least 50 olive trees belonging to the Palestinian Siam family after attacking the village of Mikhmas, northeast of occupied East Jerusalem.
Ibrahim said attacks have affected olive farming, with at least 45,000 trees destroyed across the occupied West Bank this year.
Settler violence, backed by army raids
Since October 7, 2023 there have been almost 15,000 settler attacks in the occupied West Bank, with 66 Palestinians killed, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
One such pogrom, backed by Israeli forces in the village of Marda, north of Salfit, injured a number of Palestinians picking olives on Wednesday. They were treated for tear gas inhalation by the PRCS, according to Wafa, which says Israeli forces detained at least three Palestinians.
Separately, a Palestinian was injured after being shot with live ammunition by Israeli forces during a raid near the al-Aqsa restaurant in Jenin. The injured man was taken to hospital by PRCS.
Israeli forces detained a Palestinian and imposed a curfew on residents in Burqa, as settlers raided the village east of Ramallah.

articles.summary: ‘There will be no Tel Aviv’: Egyptians threaten Israel following Smotrich Sinai comments  The Jerusalem PostEgypt rejects dragging Sinai’s name into Israeli Finance Minister’s statements, source says  Egypt TodayEgyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa issues harsh message against Israel  Egypt IndependentIsraeli minister Smotrich threatens Egypt ahead of 1973 October war anniversary  The New ArabSmotrich Threatens to Occupy Sinai and Angry Reactions in Eg &nbsp...
articles.full_text:
Egyptian media channels widely aired threats against Israel, Tel Aviv, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week as they reacted angrily to Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s warning Monday that Israel would destroy Sinai if Egypt attacked Israel, delivered during an interview with the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) news site Hashtiblach.
“What will cause Egypt not to attack us? They know that if they attack, there will be no Sinai,” Smotrich told the channel. “It won’t happen again. There is no [Menachem] Begin.”
Then-prime minister Menachem Begin made peace with Egypt by signing the historic Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty on March 26, 1979. Under the treaty, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces and civilians from the Sinai Peninsula in phases, while Egypt regained full sovereignty over the territory, and the two countries established security arrangements governing their forces in the peninsula.
“At least half of Gaza under tomorrow morning, and the same thing with Lebanon, up to 8, 9, [or] 12 kilometers that are ours. Guys, it won’t be [yours], you’re not coming back. Why? Because you started with us, and that’s the price of war,” Smotrich said.
Though his threat made clear that such an action would only be taken if Egypt attacked Israel, in the wider context of Israel’s post-October 7 security, his words were poorly received in Egypt. Egyptian parliamentarian and journalist Mustafa Bakri described the minister as an “extremist Zionist… thug” and insisted that Cairo could “crush” Israel’s military.
“[Smotrich] thinks Egypt is an open playground. I wish you would read how we crushed your army, you ignorant fool – the ones who did it once are capable of repeating it again.
“The Egyptian army is ready to confront and crush anyone whose soul dares to tamper with national security,” Bakri wrote. “You will surely be taken prisoner, and we’ll throw you in the mental hospital in Khanka. Don’t you dare overstep again, you madman [he said, addressing Smotrich].”
Egyptian TV host: Israel would pay 'heavy price' if it attacked
Egyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa, on Ala Mas’ouleety [Egyptian nightly talk show broadcast on the satellite channel Sada El Balad], also commented on Smotrich’s remarks, responding by insisting that “all 120 million Egyptians would die defending Egypt, and Israel would pay a heavy price if it took any step threatening Egyptian national security.”
Moussa noted Egypt’s success in the Yom Kippur War, during which more than 200 Israeli soldiers were taken prisoner by Egyptian forces, saying that this time there would be no hostages to exchange.
“If you act recklessly, there will be no Israel. You cannot get near an inch of Sinai, and what happened in 1967 will not be repeated with Egypt.”
“We are advocates of peace, but some extremists in the Zionist entity do not want peace. Egypt is a strong country. The war criminal says he will take Sinai. This is harassment and a threat to Egypt. We know what the lesson of 1973 was like for you,” Moussa said.
“You are an illegitimate state. We brought you back with the prisoner exchange, and after that there will be no prisoner exchange because there will be no prisoners.”
'There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport'
Amr Adib, on MBC Egypt, insisted that Cairo had actively worked to defend the border with Israel from any instability, and if the IDF attacked, “There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport, and there will be no Netanyahu.”
“Before you decide to finish us, you will be finished,” he said. “Before you throw us into the sea, you will be in the sewer.”
Egyptian political science professor Hamed Fares told Sky News Arabia that Smotrich’s comments reflected a form of “political adolescence” and demonstrated, in his view, the minister’s ignorance of the region’s power dynamics.
Fares added that he believed Smotrich’s comments, which he described as a “redline” for Egypt, reflected the finance minister’s efforts to maintain a hardline image ahead of the upcoming elections.
Fares said that by portraying neighboring countries as unstable, Smotrich was seeking to create a perceived need for territorial expansion on national security grounds.
