The programme comes as Saudi Arabia continues to expand the capacity and competitiveness of its ports and logistics network
Saudi Maritime and Logistics Congress has announced a new wave of partners, exhibitors and speakers for its 2026 edition, taking place at Jeddah Superdome on 21 and 22 October under the patronage of His Excellency Saleh Bin Nasser Al-Jasser, Minister of Transport and Logistics Services.
The 2026 edition is supported by main partners the Transport General Authority, Mawani and Aramco, founding strategic partners Bahri and Seatrade Maritime Saudi Arabia, part of Informa, and strategic partner Bassam Shipping.
More than 200 companies will exhibit across maritime equipment, port technology and logistics services, bringing together businesses involved across the shipping and logistics supply chain.The conference programme will run across two stages, with a main stage carrying the headline sessions and a focus stage running deeper technical and commercial content in parallel. More than 120 speakers will take part across five tracks covering trade corridors, port competitiveness, energy transition, infrastructure investment and maritime security.
The programme comes as Saudi Arabia continues to expand the capacity and competitiveness of its ports and logistics network. Ports overseen by Mawani handled 8.32 million TEUs in 2025, an increase of 10.58 percent year on year, while transshipment volumes rose 11.78 percent.[1]
Against that backdrop, this year’s sessions will focus on the commercial decisions facing port operators, shipowners, cargo owners, investors and their advisers as trade routes shift, infrastructure expands and the industry weighs new fuels, technologies and sources of capital.
Jay New, chief executive of King Abdullah Port, will examine what shipping lines and cargo owners need from ports before committing volume, including the case for ports developing into broader industrial and logistics hubs.
Poul Hestbæk, chief executive of Folk Maritime, will discuss how shipping lines and port operators are approaching long-term commercial decisions, with a focus on resilience, route planning and the corridors expected to support future freight growth.
Esben Poulsson, chairman at Cambiaso Risso Asia, will address risk management and commercial neutrality for operators working across multiple trade blocs.
Rania Tadros, Middle East managing partner at Stephenson Harwood, will look at liability, insurance and arbitration when cargo is delayed or diverted, as well as the role ports can play in maintaining trade continuity.
Further confirmed speakers include senior representatives from the Moroccan Ministry of Transport and Logistic, ABS, DNV Maritime, Gulf Marine Services and Jadeer Logistics.
Saudi Arabia aims to rank among the world’s top ten logistics economies by 2030 under the National Transport and Logistics Strategy. Saudi Maritime and Logistics Congress will bring together the companies and decision-makers involved in delivering that ambition, from ports and shipowners to logistics operators, financiers, engineering firms and technology providers.

articles.title: 3 years after October 7 Hamas attack: A scarred Israel, a devastated Gaza and a Middle East no longer the same - The Times of India
articles.summary: 3 years after October 7 Hamas attack: A scarred Israel, a devastated Gaza and a Middle East no longer the same  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Three years after Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the shockwaves of that day continue to shape lives, politics and security across the Middle East. What began as a devastating assault on southern Israel grew into a prolonged war in Gaza and then widened into a regional confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups.
The conflict has left behind two deeply traumatic realities - the Israeli experience of the attack, hostage-taking and continuing security fears, and the Palestinian devastation caused by the war in Gaza. Beyond the immediate human cost, the conflict has also altered alliances, weakened Iran’s regional network, changed Israel’s military calculations and disrupted diplomatic efforts across the region.
For those who lived through October 7, however, the consequences are not measured only in geopolitical shifts. They remain embedded in ordinary moments, places and memories, reminders of a day that transformed the meaning of safety, freedom and home.
“The smell of hell.”
That is how one Israeli resident describes what a barbecue now smells like.
Living close to Gaza, Deganit Bar Hay told AP the smell of burnt flesh has become a trigger, making it difficult for her to barbecue.
Benny and Maggy Solomon, parents of Oct 7 victim Hila Solomon, attend a memorial at the Nova festival site in southern Israel (Credit: AP)
Along the highway running parallel to the Gaza Strip, where people were gunned down while trying to flee on October 7, memorials now stand beside the road.
Cars smashed and riddled with bullets have been preserved elsewhere, stacked in rusting heaps. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a possible attack were disregarded, mark another set of lives lost that day.
For those who survived the attack and those who were taken hostage, the meaning of ordinary life changed too.
“Freedom has completely changed the way I see life,” Emily Damari, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and released in January 2025, told Reuters.
After captivity, she said, even opening a refrigerator or drinking cold water felt like something to be grateful for. “Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again.”
Eli Sharabi, taken hostage from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri, spent 491 days in captivity. His wife Lianne and daughters Noiya and Yahel were killed in the October 7 attack, while his brother Yossi was taken hostage and died in Gaza. Released in February 2025 emaciated after what he said was prolonged hunger, shackling and beatings, Sharabi told Reuters: “I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do.”
Three years later, those memories remain raw in Israel. But there is another landscape of memory just across the border.
In Gaza, children are growing up with different reminders of the same war - lost parents, amputations, displacement, damaged homes and years without anything resembling a normal childhood. DW reported the stories of 15-year-old Mahmoud Abu Shadaq, recovering from injuries caused by an airstrike, and eight-year-old Layan Abed, who lost her father during the conflict.
Aid groups are providing rehabilitation and mental-health support, but the scars are likely to outlast the fighting.
That is the paradox at the heart of the three years since October 7.
One attack produced two vastly different but deeply traumatic legacies - the Israeli trauma of the assault and hostage-taking, and the Palestinian devastation that followed Israel's military campaign in Gaza.
And the consequences did not stop at Gaza's borders.
What began with Hamas's assault on southern Israel became a war in Gaza, then a wider confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups across the region. It has altered Israel's security doctrine, weakened Iran's regional network, unsettled Arab states, disrupted diplomacy and pushed the Middle East into a new and still uncertain balance of power.
Three years on, the question is no longer simply what happened on October 7. It is what October 7 set in motion.
October 7, 2023: Day the ‘iron’ wall broke
Just before 6.30am on October 7, 2023, Israel’s much-vaunted “iron wall” along Gaza began to fail. Explosives dropped by drones knocked out communication towers and remote-controlled guns, while snipers targeted sensors and cameras. Israeli defenders were left staring at blank screens as roughly 2,200 rockets rained towards southern and central Israel.
A minute-by-minute look at how the October 7 assault broke through Israel’s border defences.
Then came the breach. Hamas fighters cut through the 20-foot-high fence or blew openings into it. Motorbikes, pickup trucks and bulldozers poured through, followed by hundreds of armed men. Others arrived on motorised paragliders. About 30 breaches were eventually made, allowing an estimated 1,500 fighters into Israel, The Guardian reported.
It was more than a fence being breached. It was the collapse of an assumption — that Israel’s technology, intelligence and military superiority had made a large-scale assault from Gaza almost impossible.
“We have decided to put an end to all of the occupation’s crimes,” Hamas commander Mohammed Deif announced as the attack began, declaring the “al-Aqsa deluge”.
Within hours, the assault had turned deadly. Fighters stormed military positions and nearby communities, reaching the Supernova music festival, where at least 260 people were killed and others taken hostage. In kibbutzim such as Be’eri, residents barricaded themselves inside reinforced rooms as gunmen moved through the communities. At Zikim, soldiers at a military base were overwhelmed before reinforcements arrived.

The scale of the failure soon became clear.
Israeli intelligence had detected increased communications activity among militants in Gaza before the attack. Egyptian security services had also warned of an impending event. But Israeli officials assessed the activity as connected to a military exercise and decided that the alert level did not need to be raised, The Guardian reported. Three surveillance balloons used to monitor the border had also broken down and had not been replaced.
The result was a catastrophic intelligence and preparedness failure: a border designed to keep Gaza's militants out became a route into Israel, while the forces meant to respond were caught unprepared.
For people inside the communities along the border, the technological failure quickly became intensely personal.
In Nirim, resident Eldad Hess and his family hid inside a reinforced shelter as gunfire erupted outside. “Ten minutes later we heard automatic rifle shots outside the house,” Hess told The Guardian. “I understood what was happening but in my heart I couldn't believe what was happening.”
His family survived. Others did not.
By late morning, Israel had declared war. At 10.34am, Israeli strikes began hitting Gaza. At 11.35am, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Israelis: “Citizens of Israel, we are at war. Not an operation, not a round – at war.”
The language of the conflict changed almost as quickly as its geography.
The attack had begun as a meticulously planned assault on southern Israel. Within hours, it had become the opening act of a war that would transform Gaza, redraw Israel's security calculations and eventually pull much of the Middle East into its orbit.
Palestinian children walk amid the rubble of buildings destroyed during Gaza war (Credit: Reuters)
Gaza became war's price, and its unfinished question
The military campaign that followed October 7 devastated Gaza.
Entire neighbourhoods were destroyed, millions were displaced and a generation of children has grown up amid death, injury and uncertainty. The humanitarian crisis became one of the defining consequences of the war.
Even after a ceasefire agreement in October 2025 secured the release of the remaining hostages and hundreds of Palestinian prisoners and detainees, the larger Gaza question remained unresolved.
According to Reuters, Israeli strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. Gaza's health ministry says at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the truce, while Israel says its strikes target Hamas and accuses the group of trying to rearm and carry out attacks. Hamas denies the accusation.
Meanwhile, Israel's effective control over Gaza has expanded to around two-thirds of the enclave, Reuters reported. The advance of the Israeli-controlled “yellow line” has squeezed Gaza's roughly 2 million residents into a shrinking coastal area where many live in tents or damaged buildings.
The numbers tell one part of the story. The more difficult question is what happens next.
Trump's plan envisaged Hamas disarming, Israeli forces gradually withdrawing, an International Stabilization Force taking over security and a new Palestinian technocratic administration governing Gaza.
None of those pieces has fully fallen into place.
The proposed force has a commander and commitments from several countries but has yet to be assembled. A Palestinian technocratic governing body appointed in January has yet to enter Gaza. Hamas has indicated a willingness to hand its weapons over for storage under a US-backed Palestinian administration, but Israel has rejected any withdrawal before complete disarmament.
And reconstruction is barely beginning.
A $2.45 billion plan announced by the Board of Peace in September is dwarfed by an EU-UN estimate of $71.4 billion needed for recovery and reconstruction over the next decade, Reuters reported.
The war may have ended in parts of Gaza. The question of what Gaza becomes has not.

articles.title: Moody’s: Spending Restraint to Strengthen Saudi Arabia’s Fiscal Recovery in 2027 - ASHARQ AL-AWSAT English
articles.summary: Moody’s: Spending Restraint to Strengthen Saudi Arabia’s Fiscal Recovery in 2027  ASHARQ AL-AWSAT English
articles.full_text:
Credit rating agency Moody’s said on Tuesday that the fiscal recovery planned for Saudi Arabia in 2027 supports its view that prudent fiscal management will remain a key factor in spending and borrowing decisions.
The agency also noted that reprioritizing state investments could preserve fiscal space while economic diversification continues.
Commenting on Saudi Arabia’s Pre-Budget Statement for next year, the rating agency said that prolonged trade disruptions and additional spending have limited the fiscal improvement it previously expected.
However, it said, Saudi Arabia’s move to rein in spending in 2027 reinforces its view that prudent fiscal management will remain a cornerstone of spending and borrowing decisions.
For 2027, the government projects a spending decrease to SAR 1.392 trillion ($371.2 billion), alongside a 1% rise in revenue to SAR 1.202 trillion ($320.5 billion); this would narrow the projected deficit to around SAR 191 billion ($50.7 billion), equivalent to 3.6% of GDP.
Moody’s said the government's ability to reprioritize investments linked to Saudi Vision 2030 could preserve fiscal space while economic diversification continues. Focusing resources on projects with strong returns would likely help reconcile growth objectives with spending restraint.
As for oil, the agency expected that disruptions to strategic shipping routes will persist through the end of the first half of 2027, which could affect oil production. However, it noted that higher oil prices have cushioned the impact of lower production and exports in recent months.
Saudi Arabia's real GDP is expected to contract 3.6% in 2026, largely because of a sharp decline in oil activity, even as the non-oil economy continues to expand, according to the Ministry of Finance's Pre-Budget Statement for 2027.
The Ministry estimates that oil activity will decline by around 21.8% this year, while non-oil activities are expected to grow 3.2%, helping cushion the impact of lower oil output on the wider economy.
Non-oil activity grew 1.8% in the first half of 2026, lifting its contribution to GDP to a record 57.3%, the statement said.
Moody’s review reflects a credit assessment of the Pre-Budget Statement for 2027 that places more emphasis on the government's capability to recalibrate investment and prioritize spending efficiency while explicitly preserving its overarching economic diversification goals. This, it said, would help preserve fiscal flexibility amid geopolitical strains and global market uncertainties.

articles.title: Hormuz ship attacks surge: Are increased oil exports sustainable? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Hormuz ship attacks surge: Are increased oil exports sustainable?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Oil exports from the Gulf have resumed significantly in recent days, despite a surge in attacks on ships around the Strait of Hormuz, maritime experts and trackers say.
Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, maritime intelligence firm Kpler reported.
However, the recovery has come as attacks on tankers increase and shipping companies face higher freight, insurance and security costs.
On Tuesday, 12 crew members on a Panama-flagged tanker were injured in an attack by an unknown projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, India’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.
In retaliation for US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait, while Washington has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.
So, how are ships getting through the strait, and how long can producers maintain the increased flow through one of the world’s most important energy corridors while attacks and harassment of ships continue?
What do we know about the recent attacks on ships?
The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz has continued to deteriorate even as more oil moves out of the region.
At least seven incidents involving tankers have been reported in the past week, according to shipping intelligence service Marisks.
The Kuwaiti-flagged Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) MT Kazimah III caught fire after being struck on October 1 while travelling through the strait, causing a fire on board. Five staff were safely rescued following the incident.
On October 4, the Liberian-flagged Aframax tanker Lipsi was struck northeast of Oman’s Jazirat Umm al-Fayarin, damaging its engine room, with no casualties reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or the Gulf of Aden, where Iran-backed Houthis are targeting Saudi-linked shipping, since October 2.
Threats continued on Monday, when a tanker entering the Hormuz strait near Oman was hailed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and ordered to turn around or risk attack, according to UKMTO.
How much oil is getting through the Hormuz Strait?
Despite those attacks, oil exports from the region have risen dramatically.
According to provisional data from Kpler, the seven-day moving average for Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with an average of about 18 million bpd during the 12 months before the war.
Vortexa separately estimated that the 14-day moving average for Middle East crude and condensate exports had reached 18.6 million bpd.
However, not all of that oil is actually being shipped through Hormuz.
Kpler estimates that about 40 percent of oil exports now bypass the strait, while much of the crude that does cross is transferred between tankers offshore.
Partly as a result of the increased oil exports, oil prices continue to fall, with Brent crude – the global benchmark – dropping 0.75 percent to $99.57 a barrel on Tuesday. US West Texas Intermediate crude also fell 1.2 percent to $88.37 a barrel, according to data from Oilprice.com.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly taken credit for the apparent increase in oil flows, boasting that Washington controls the strait and that US forces were succeeding in protecting vessels passing through Hormuz.
Iran has disputed claims that oil flow through the key waterway has increased, saying the amount passing was “negligible” and that it still has effective control of the strait.
How are oil exports bypassing Hormuz?
The recovery of oil exports has been made possible largely by Saudi Arabia’s use of alternative export infrastructure and an increasingly complex system for moving crude around Hormuz.
“The increasing availability of crude oil from the Middle East is due to two factors: the effective use of the East-West pipeline by Saudi Arabia and ship-to-ship transfer around the Strait of Hormuz,” Tamas Varga, an analyst at PVM Oil Associates, told Al Jazeera.
Saudi’s East-West pipeline carries oil from fields in the east of the country to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the West.
Ship-to-ship transfers happen when smaller shuttle boats, which often turn off their transponders to make them hard to detect, physically transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz, before offloading their cargoes onto larger tankers waiting just beyond it.
Is this sustainable?
Varga said current flows could be maintained as long as those methods and routes remain secure.
Saudi’s East-West pipeline has already suffered temporary closures as a result of drone strikes, such as those launched by Iran-backed groups in Iraq in September.
“The flow will be sustainable unless attacks on ships and shipping lanes or on the pipeline resume, something that does not seem imminent at the moment but could happen at any time if geopolitical tensions flare up,” he said.
But maintaining those flows is also putting pressure on the shipping system.
“The shuttle system in the Gulf is doing wonders in getting oil out, but it requires plenty of ships,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
That demand has pushed freight costs higher and reduced tanker availability elsewhere, while Asian buyers are increasingly having to source crude from further afield, he added.
“Previously a supply story, this is now one about the underlying mechanics of shipping,” Beauchamp said. “Ships don’t get built overnight.”
Varga said oil prices also remain comparatively high – currently hovering just less than $100 a barrel compared with around $72 before the war broke out – because of increased shipping and insurance costs.
Last week, members of the Group of Seven (G7) announced they would release up to 100 million barrels of strategic oil reserves, including diesel, in a bid to control prices. Further releases of crude and diesel from strategic reserves could also ease prices, but with global inventories already thin, another deterioration in Middle East security could quickly push them higher again.
“Only a sustainable and credible peace deal between the US and Iran and the subsequent permanent and unconditional reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would re-establish the pre-conflict status quo,” Varga said.
On Monday, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser warned that the effects of the disruption could last well beyond the reopening of Hormuz, even if it does happen.
Speaking at the Energy Intelligence conference in London, Nasser said nearly three billion barrels of oil supply had been lost since the conflict began at the end of February and that rebuilding depleted inventories while meeting demand could take as long as two years.
“The system is already straining,” he added.

articles.title: 3 Energy Stocks Positioned for Extended Iran-War Volatility - TradingView
articles.summary: 3 Energy Stocks Positioned for Extended Iran-War Volatility  TradingView

The prolonged Iran conflict has reshaped global energy markets beyond a simple rise in crude prices. Middle Eastern oil flows have started recovering as producers find alternative ways to move barrels, but shipping disruptions, high freight costs, tight refined-product supplies and pressure on liquefied natural gas (LNG) availability continue to keep the market unsettled.
Brent crude recently moved back around $100 per barrel after a sharp pullback, highlighting how quickly prices are reacting to changes in Gulf exports, military developments and shipping conditions. This volatility makes company-specific positioning increasingly important.
Companies with limited exposure to disrupted Middle Eastern assets, strong LNG export capacity or diversified global operations may be better placed to navigate an extended conflict. Against this backdrop, Chevron Corporation CVX, Cheniere Energy, Inc. LNG and Shell plc SHEL stand out for different reasons.
Energy Markets Remain Under Pressure
The global oil market has adjusted to the disruption faster than initially expected. Middle Eastern crude exports have rebounded as producers increasingly rely on pipelines, shuttle tankers and ship-to-ship transfers to move barrels around affected shipping routes.
However, the recovery has been uneven. Refined-product markets remain tight, particularly diesel, while higher freight costs and limited tanker availability continue to complicate global energy flows.
LNG has also become an important part of the supply story. Disruptions to Qatari production have increased the strategic value of suppliers outside the Middle East, particularly U.S. exporters. Meanwhile, companies with strong U.S. oil production can participate in elevated global prices while avoiding heavy dependence on Persian Gulf supply routes.
Chevron: Diversified Production Supports Resilience
Chevron is well positioned to benefit from stronger crude prices while limiting direct exposure to the Middle East. Much of the company’s production growth is coming from the United States and Guyana.
Chevron has built a large presence in the Permian Basin, while its acquisition of Hess added a 30% interest in Guyana’s Stabroek Block. Guyana has emerged as a major source of new oil supply outside the Middle East, strengthening Chevron’s geographic diversification.
The Hess acquisition, combined with continued growth from U.S. operations, has expanded Chevron’s overall production base. The company also maintains a sizable downstream business, giving it exposure to stronger refining conditions when global fuel inventories tighten.
This positioning matters during a prolonged conflict. Higher crude prices can support upstream earnings, while Chevron’s limited dependence on Middle Eastern production reduces the risk that regional disruptions erase those gains.
Strong cash generation also provides flexibility to fund projects, manage debt and maintain shareholder distributions through volatile commodity cycles.
For investors, Chevron’s appeal therefore extends beyond higher oil prices. Its expanding U.S. and Guyana operations provide meaningful production exposure while keeping direct conflict-related operating risks relatively contained. CVX currently carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

Cheniere Energy: U.S. LNG Gains Strategic Importance
Cheniere Energy offers a different way to participate in the changing energy landscape. Rather than relying mainly on crude prices, the company benefits from its position as a leading U.S. LNG exporter.
That role has become more important as disruptions to Middle Eastern LNG production encourage buyers to diversify supply.
Cheniere Energy recently completed the Corpus Christi Stage 3 project, increasing LNG production capacity across Corpus Christi and Sabine Pass by more than 20% to roughly 56 million tonnes per annum.
The added capacity arrives at an opportune time. Reduced Qatari LNG availability has increased demand for reliable suppliers capable of delivering cargoes to Europe, Asia and other major consuming regions.
Cheniere Energy is also pursuing additional LNG capacity through further development opportunities at Corpus Christi and Sabine Pass, subject to regulatory and investment approvals.
The company had already raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA and distributable cash flow outlook before the latest tightening in global LNG supplies. Its expanded infrastructure and contracted customer base provide a strong foundation to serve growing demand.
For Cheniere Energy, the prolonged Iran conflict creates an opportunity tied more to energy security than short-term gas-price movements. If buyers continue seeking geographically diversified supplies, U.S. LNG could become increasingly important, potentially supporting additional long-term contracts. Cheniere Energy currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).
Shell: Integrated Model Provides a Cushion
Shell faces greater direct Middle Eastern exposure than Chevron or Cheniere Energy, making its investment case more complicated.
The company has significant operations in Qatar and elsewhere in the region, and the conflict has already affected some assets. Damage to one processing train at the Pearl gas-to-liquids facility highlights the operational risks associated with prolonged regional instability.
However, Shell’s diversified global business provides several potential offsets.
The company operates across upstream oil and gas, LNG, refining, chemicals and commodity trading. This integrated structure allows stronger performance in one segment to help cushion weakness elsewhere.
Shell’s LNG trading capabilities are particularly valuable during periods of supply disruption. The company can redirect cargoes across regions and respond to changing price differentials, helping it capture value from market volatility.
Its refining operations provide another buffer. Tight diesel and fuel markets can support refining margins, adding an earnings stream beyond upstream production.
Still, Shell carries greater conflict-related risk than Chevron because of its Gulf exposure. Continued instability could affect production and project schedules. Yet its diversified portfolio reduces dependence on any single region or commodity. SHEL carries a Zacks Rank #3 at present.
Why These Three Stocks Stand Out
Chevron, Cheniere Energy and Shell provide three different ways to navigate the same geopolitical disruption.
Chevron combines higher oil-price exposure with growing production in the United States and Guyana. Cheniere Energy benefits from the rising strategic importance of U.S. LNG as buyers seek alternatives to Middle Eastern supply. Shell carries greater Gulf exposure but can rely on its global LNG, trading, refining and upstream businesses to offset part of the impact.
The key advantage shared by all three is operating flexibility. As the Iran conflict continues to reshape global trade routes and energy availability, companies with diversified production, export infrastructure and multiple earnings streams may be better positioned to remain resilient through an extended period of volatility.

articles.title: Why An Iran Us Deal Is Still Possible If Washington Plays By The Rules - ИФЗ РАН
articles.summary: Why An Iran Us Deal Is Still Possible If Washington Plays By The Rules  ИФЗ РАН
articles.full_text:
Diplomatic stalemates rarely end with fireworks. They drag on through carefully worded statements, state media broadcasts, and stubborn positioning. Tehran recently made headlines through the Iranian Students' News Agency (ISNA) by signaling that a renewed diplomatic accord with Washington isn't impossible. The catch? The United States has to abide by international law and respect prior commitments.
If you've followed geopolitical negotiations for more than five minutes, you know this rhetoric is vintage foreign policy theater. Yet, beneath the predictable posturing lies a real question about what it would actually take to revive stalled nuclear talks or stabilize the Middle East. Let's look past the press releases and break down what's really happening.
What Tehran Actually Means by Abiding by Law
When Iranian officials talk about the law, they aren't speaking abstractly. They are referring to specific grievances tied to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) and the unilateral withdrawal by Washington years ago. From Tehran's perspective, trust was broken when sanctions snapped back into place despite international compliance reports confirming Iranian adherence to the accord at the time.
You can't expect a sovereign state to jump back to the negotiating table without guarantees that the next agreement won't evaporate the moment a new administration takes office in the White House. That's the core hurdle. Domestic political cycles in Western democracies make long-term international treaties fragile. Tehran wants binding legal assurances, while Washington faces constitutional hurdles that make treaty ratification nearly impossible without Senate approval—something neither political party is likely to secure for an Iran deal anytime soon.
The Economic Realities Driving the Talk
Sanctions haven't destroyed the Iranian economy, but they've certainly made life difficult for everyday citizens while reorienting trade routes toward neighbors and eastern partners like China and Russia. Inflation hurts. Currency devaluation hurts.
At the same time, complete isolation hasn't worked either. Tehran has managed to keep oil flowing through creative shipping maneuvers and alternative financial channels. This reality gives negotiators on both sides a weird kind of leverage. Iran isn't begging for relief from a position of total collapse, and Washington isn't facing immediate pressure to lift sanctions unless domestic inflation or regional escalation forces their hand.
When ISNA floats stories about a potential deal being within reach, it's a signal to domestic hardliners and foreign capitals alike. It says, "We aren't closed for business, but we won't negotiate under duress."
Why Washington Won't Move Easily
On the other side of the globe, US foreign policy remains paralyzed by domestic election cycles and intense congressional skepticism. Any administration attempting to ease sanctions or strike a new diplomatic framework faces immediate bipartisan backlash. Lawmakers point to regional proxies, human rights concerns, and advanced uranium enrichment levels as absolute dealbreakers.
Trust is a two-way street. Washington argues that Tehran's continued expansion of its nuclear program beyond agreed-upon limits makes diplomatic goodwill impossible. You hear Washington insiders ask a straightforward question: why reward escalation with concessions?
This creates a classic chicken-and-egg dilemma. Tehran demands sanctions relief first to prove good faith. Washington demands nuclear rollbacks first to verify compliance. Until one side blinks or external pressures shift the calculus, statements via state news agencies will remain just that—words on a screen.
What to Watch Next in the Diplomatic Chessboard
If you want to know whether a real breakthrough is happening, ignore the public statements altogether. Watch the back-channel mediators. Oman and Qatar have historically played crucial roles in passing messages between Washington and Tehran without the noise of public media.
Look for quiet prisoner swaps, unfreezing of restricted funds in third-party banks, or subtle adjustments at International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) monitoring sites. Those operational shifts tell you far more than any ISNA report or congressional hearing ever will.
The door to diplomacy is open a crack, but neither side is willing to walk through it without holding a heavy shield.

Three people were killed in attacks targeting two airports in Saudi Arabia, the kingdom’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said Wednesday.
The Saudi authorities did not blame any party for the attacks at Abha and Riyadh’s King Khalid international airports, but Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed earlier that they carried out attacks against the two airports.
The attack on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and wounded 28 other people, while the attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people, officials said.
As the Saudi capital is targeted again, new cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport. The kingdom, the world’s top oil exporter, has seen oil and military assets targeted in recent days.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones against King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Flights were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24.
Now Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces have launched a major ground and air offensive aimed at retaking territory that the rebels seized a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Those positions gave the Houthis better surveillance as they pursue a blockade of Saudi-linked shipping. On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition recaptured several key areas around the strait, through which about 12% of global trade transits.
"The Houthis believe that they can maximize Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an analysis.
The Houthi spokesperson said they also targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, a frequent target of rebel drones and missiles. The rebels also claimed to hit an air base in the city of Khamis Mushait and two military bases in Najran and Asir. All are in the southwest, near the Yemeni border.
Inside Yemen, fighting has centered in and around the crucial town of Dhubab, some 54 kilometers (33.5 miles) south of the port city of Mokha that the rebels seized last month, according to both the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government.

The U.S. and Greece announced $4 billion in Foreign Military Sales on Wednesday to support Athens’ long-term defense plans as the NATO allies moved to expand security and economic cooperation.
The announcement came after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis presided over the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue in Athens, according to a joint statement released by the U.S. State Department.
The two sides said the military sales would support Greece's defense plans and deepen interoperability, while they would also explore further cooperation between their defense industries, including in innovative technologies.
They also finalized Greece's participation in the U.S. National Guard Bureau's State Partnership Program with Florida and said interoperability would be enhanced through the provision of Stryker vehicles to Greece.
Washington and Athens, according to the statement, also agreed to expand law enforcement and counterterrorism cooperation and reiterated their commitment to addressing irregular migration.

articles.title: RSF strikes kill 4 in SE Sudan as al-Burhan vows to continue fight
articles.summary: Paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) drone strikes targeting civilian areas in Damazin, the capital of Sudan’s Blue Nile state, killed at least four civilians and injured dozens...
articles.full_text:
Paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) drone strikes targeting civilian areas in Damazin, the capital of Sudan’s Blue Nile state, killed at least four civilians and injured dozens Wednesday, according to two rights groups.
The Emergency Lawyers Committee said in a statement that RSF drones targeted civilian sites in Damazin early Wednesday, including homes and a mosque.
"The attack killed four women in the al-Hijra neighborhood and injured dozens of civilians," the committee said.
It warned against continued attacks on civilian sites, saying that "deliberately directing attacks against civilians or civilian objects constitutes a serious violation of international humanitarian law."
The committee called for "an immediate halt to the attacks and for those responsible to be held accountable."
Meanwhile, the Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative, a local civil society group, condemned "the attack carried out by the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), using drones against residential neighborhoods in Damazin."
The initiative expressed "deep concern over the targeting of civilian sites and places of worship."
The RSF did not immediately comment on the report. However, Sudanese authorities and human rights groups have repeatedly accused the group of targeting civilians, a charge the RSF has denied.
The three states of the Kordofan region – North, West and South Kordofan – have witnessed clashes between the army and the RSF since October 2025.
On Aug. 24, the U.N. said 1,100 civilians had been killed in drone attacks in Sudan between January and June this year.
Earlier Tuesday, Sudanese Sovereign Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan vowed to continue a military campaign against the RSF until "every inch” of the country is retaken, according to media reports.
Burhan made the remarks while addressing a public gathering in Village 5 in the Merowe locality in Northern State, the Sudan News Agency reported.
He renewed the armed forces' determination to press ahead with the "military option" until the entire country is cleared of the RSF.
He reiterated the position of the government and military rejecting negotiations with the RSF and said efforts will continue to restore security and stability and preserve Sudan's unity.
The government has repeatedly rejected any political settlement with the RSF that it said will place "a sovereign state and a rebel militia" on equal footing.
It maintains that any truce or dialogue must be based on conditions, including the RSF's withdrawal from cities and public institutions, the handover of weapons, the regrouping of its forces in designated camps and accountability for those accused of violations.
Sudan has been engulfed in war between the army and the RSF since April 2023 because of a dispute related to integrating the paramilitary force into the military.
The conflict has triggered famine conditions in parts of the country, killed tens of thousands and displaced 13 million, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

articles.title: Rubio urges West to return to its ‘civilizational roots’
articles.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for the nations of the West to return to their civilizational roots and restore the values that drove the rise of Europe and North Americ...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for the nations of the West to return to their civilizational roots and restore the values that drove the rise of Europe and North America to global dominance for centuries.
In Athens to discuss deepening economic, energy and security cooperation with Greece, Rubio delivered a speech later Wednesday near the ruins of the Acropolis, a widely recognizable symbol of the city's ancient civilization associated with the creation of popular participatory government and the social contract.
Rubio aimed to remind listeners of qualities he says were born in Greece and later defined the West, such as curiosity, courage, ambition, a restless spirit of exploration and a drive to discover the unknown.
"It has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the 'global community' over one's own people. And I think here, too, we have much more to learn from the men of Ancient Greece. They knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else," Rubio said.
"Today, we find ourselves at a crossroads," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century. The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all."
Rubio is seen by many as the gentle face of the Trump administration and has been frequently dispatched to clarify or otherwise address concerns about the president's frequently undiplomatic statements.
Rubio, along with Vice President JD Vance, is seen as one of the leading contenders to assume Trump's mantle at the top of the Republican Party, which faces stiff challenges in next month's congressional midterm elections. Republican Party, which faces stiff challenges in next month's congressional midterm elections.
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused countries in Europe of backsliding on their traditional values and democratic principles by stifling the free speech of conservatives and falling short on commitments to international partners like the United States.
Many of those countries have rejected the complaints and accused the U.S. under Trump of being guilty of similar behavior and worse with its staunch anti-immigration stance that some believe is racist.
Ahead of his visit to Athens, about 1,500 people gathered to protest Rubio's presence and the war in Iran, chanting "American killers!"
The demonstration was organized by a communist labor union and other left-wing groups and was held ahead of extensive road closures planned in Athens. Organizers said similar protests were held in at least 12 other Greek cities. Police banned public demonstrations Wednesday in central.
Rubio is on the second leg of a three-nation tour of NATO allies that has already taken him to Iceland and will end in Portugal on Thursday. The trip is aimed at reassuring U.S. partners that the Trump administration is committed to their success and security despite what has been an often brusque and sometimes rude approach to traditional friends that has stirred unease.
Rubio began emphasizing historical themes on Thursday, when he met Iceland's foreign minister at the site of the landmark 1986 summit between former President Ronald Reagan and then Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, a meeting that many believe marked the beginning of the end of the Cold War and was a catalyst for the eventual dissolution of the Soviet Union.
It remains unclear what impact Rubio's visits will have, although on Tuesday in Reykjavik, he sought to reassure Iceland that President Donald Trump's administration has no designs on the island. Rather, he said the U.S. shares Iceland's deep concerns about Arctic security as tensions between the U.S. and Russia rise in the High North and elsewhere.
Iceland has been uneasy about Trump's intentions toward it after he posted a map showing the colors of the U.S. flag sprawling across all of North America and extending to Iceland and Greenland. That wariness has persisted despite an agreement last month to increase the U.S. presence in the neighboring Danish territory of Greenland that appears to have ended Trump's demands for the U.S. to take full control of the island.
But after Rubio's talks in Reykjavik, those tensions appeared to be on the wane. Rubio said the United States would not do anything in Iceland without Iceland's consent.
Before delivering his speech in Athens, Rubio declined to comment when he was asked about allegations of misconduct leveled at U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.
At a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister, Rubio said he would not address the matter while visiting a foreign country, but added: "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
The top Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations and House Foreign Affairs committees, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and Rep. Gregory Meeks, have initiated probes into claims reported last month by the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle acted improperly while serving as the top U.S. envoy to Greece.
The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing, and Rubio has defended her before.

articles.title: Over 20,000 unaccompanied minors reached Europe in 2025: UN
articles.summary: More than 20,000 unaccompanied minors reached Europe through mixed migration routes in 2025, making up nearly two-thirds of the 31,100 children who arrived during the year, U.N. ag...
articles.full_text:
More than 20,000 unaccompanied minors reached Europe through mixed migration routes in 2025, making up nearly two-thirds of the 31,100 children who arrived during the year, U.N. agencies said.
A joint report by the International Organization for Migration, International Organization of Migration (IOM), UNHCR and UNICEF found overall child arrivals by sea and land fell 25% from 2024.
The share recorded as unaccompanied, however, rose to 67% from 51% a year earlier, according to the report.
The highest proportions were recorded in Italy and Spain, where 86% of child arrivals were unaccompanied.
IOM Director General Amy Pope warned that limited safe pathways leave children exposed to smugglers, violence and exploitation.
"Children are making difficult and dangerous journeys without a parent or guardian by their side," Pope said, calling for greater cross-border cooperation to protect them.
"No child should have to face these risks alone," she said. "Our shared responsibility is to work across borders to protect them, uphold their rights, and provide the care and support they need."
Among more than 4,600 adolescents and young adults interviewed along Mediterranean, West African Atlantic and Western Balkan routes, nearly half of those asked about their experiences reported physical violence.
On the Central Mediterranean route, 28% said they had been held against their will, while 17% reported being forced to work, according to the report.
Meanwhile, the number of children undergoing refugee resettlement procedures to Europe fell to 3,400 in 2025 from 8,900 a year earlier.
Separately, only 199 children were relocated between European states under the Voluntary Solidarity Mechanism, down 67%, the report said.
None of the relocated children was unaccompanied.
The IOM urged EU member states to "put the best interests of the child at the centre of every decision, to guarantee timely access to services, and never to detain children for immigration purposes."
"Unaccompanied and separated children should have immediate access to legal representation," the agency said.

articles.title: WHO urges Russia to release more info on plague institute death
articles.summary: The World Health Organization said Wednesday it requested information from Russia regarding the death of a plague institute worker in Siberia, but the Kremlin accused the media of...
articles.full_text:
The World Health Organization said Wednesday it requested information from Russia regarding the death of a plague institute worker in Siberia, but the Kremlin accused the media of spreading lies and insisted it had shared all known details.
Russian authorities say the 28-year-old laboratory worker died Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from U.S. President Donald Trump, and which saw around 200 people initially placed in quarantine.
Russia's health watchdog said Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, and a local official said that 60% of those placed in quarantine had been released.
But Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director general of the WHO in Geneva, said in a statement on X that his organization needed more information from Russia to fully understand what had happened.
"WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause," he said.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."
The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures.
When asked about the WHO's request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it came to using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
"There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," said Peskov.
He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters comment request on Wednesday about the WHO's questions.
Some Western media outlets have reported – citing unnamed "Russian media" – that a second person in Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague.
Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died although some bloggers on social media were making – without evidence – such assertions.
Contacted by Reuters, the WHO said it had nothing further to add on the matter beyond what Tedros – who was due to give a press conference later Wednesday – had already posted on X.
Tedros' call for more information echoed that of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio who has said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident.
While Russia's health watchdog has said that Shipilova died after contracting pneumonia, it has not publicly explained what caused it or how she fell ill.
Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or COVID-19.

articles.title: US troops slapped with curfew, alcohol ban over Okinawa murder
articles.summary: U.S. forces on Okinawa were hit with a 48-hour alcohol ban and a 30-day curfew Wednesday following the murder of a woman allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine. The case has triggere...
articles.full_text:
U.S. forces on Okinawa were hit with a 48-hour alcohol ban and a 30-day curfew Wednesday following the murder of a woman allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine.
The case has triggered outrage in Japan, where any crimes involving U.S. forces have long inflamed criticism of the troops' presence.
Genta Koja, the governor of Okinawa – where the bulk of the 54,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan are based – told Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi during a meeting in Tokyo Wednesday that there was an "urgent need to reduce base-related burdens" on the island, without providing specifics.
"The robbery-murder this time hugely shocked local residents," he said, requesting a committee be convened swiftly to discuss the issue.
Earlier Benjamin T. Watson, Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, announced a "complete prohibition of alcohol consumption on or off base" starting Wednesday.
Watson said that the 48-hour period – described as "an operational pause" – would give commanders the time to lead training with all service members on "standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community."
Operations will cease during this period and "we will not allow off-base liberty," said Watson in a statement posted on X late Tuesday.
The lieutenant general, the most senior U.S. military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day "period of reflection" beginning Friday.
"During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500."
Police said Sunday that a US Marine stationed on Okinawa was arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city of Naha and stealing her wallet.
Local media reported she was choked to death and that the Marine is denying the allegations.
The United States has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
Koja, who won the gubernatorial election last month, is the first Okinawa leader in 12 years who approved of a contentious U.S. military base relocation plan.
The central government plan is to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but move it to a less populated location.
On Wednesday, Koja also met Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi in Tokyo where he said the murder case had "caused deep anxiety" among Okinawa residents.
"The prefectural government has repeatedly demanded that the U.S. military take measures to prevent a recurrence every time an incident occurs, but the fact that such an incident has happened again forces us to conclude that discipline within the U.S. forces and their human rights education are not functioning at all," he told Koizumi.
Koizumi said that he would "advance discussions with the United States on how to implement effective measures" to prevent such incidents occurring.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, U.S. Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated U.S. Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

articles.title: France stops stun grenade, tear gas use to quell student protests
articles.summary: France has suspended the use of police stun grenades and tear gas at student-led protests, the interior minister said Wednesday, following allegations of brutality during days of v...
articles.full_text:
France has suspended the use of police stun grenades and tear gas at student-led protests, the interior minister said Wednesday, following allegations of brutality during days of violent nationwide demonstrations.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across France Tuesday demanding better conditions in high schools, which prompted President Emmanuel Macron to hold an emergency meeting with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis.
Lecornu will make a public address later Wednesday on the school protests as well as the country's finances, his office said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, meanwhile, told radio broadcaster RTL early Wednesday that he had suspended the police's use of stun grenades at the protests.
A 15-year-old lost a hand Monday after police fired a stun grenade while a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged Tuesday over that incident.
Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct since the protests began, Nunez said.
The protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages.
Parents, teachers and union workers joined the demonstrations in the capital Paris and other cities Tuesday, amid accusations of police using disproportionate force.
Sporadic violent clashes have broken out between police and protesters at what otherwise have been largely peaceful demonstrations.
Lecornu on Tuesday condemned the violence and told lawmakers the violence would not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters.
More than 6,500 people, mostly minors, have been arrested.

articles.title: Massive Russian overnight strikes kill at least 20 across Ukraine
articles.summary: Massive Russian drone and missile barrage killed at least 20 people across Ukraine overnight into Wednesday, damaging residential buildings, industrial facilities and infrastructur...
articles.full_text:
Massive Russian drone and missile barrage killed at least 20 people across Ukraine overnight into Wednesday, damaging residential buildings, industrial facilities and infrastructure, officials said.
Emergency services picked through the rubble of the flattened five-story building in Pryluky, in the Chernigiv region, in a frantic search for survivors.
But hopes faded as the toll jumped by early afternoon.
"The death toll ... has risen to 14, including four children," the state emergency services said. "Fifty people were wounded, including seven children."
Fifteen people, including a child, were rescued, they wrote on Telegram.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned the public Tuesday night that Russia was planning "massive" strikes, particularly against the country's energy infrastructure.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," he said Wednesday, calling it "one of the most vile strikes" in the nearly five-year conflict.
Two people were killed when missiles slammed into high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others lost their lives in Oleksandriya, he added.
In the capital, Kyiv, strikes killed two people.
Kyiv has come under increased attack in recent weeks as winter approaches, with air raid sirens wailing nearly constantly to warn of incoming Russian strikes.
Residents hunkered down in subway stations overnight, hauling duffel bags, sleeping mats and blankets, after air alerts sounded warning of attacks.
"We grabbed our things and came here, we live right next door," Iryna Rybalchenko, who works in a bank, told AFP, sitting on the platform wrapped in a dark hoodie and surrounded by bags.
"The whole of Kyiv is in a state of fear. We were stuck at work today and everyone – our group chats, our bosses – were messaging us to be careful."
Russia launched at least 50 missiles and 130 drones overnight against several regions including Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Poltava, Ukraine's air force said.
Zelenskyy said that although some were shot down, ballistic missiles were "the greatest challenge," and new air defenses were "a vital necessity" to help Ukraine defend itself.
The two victims in Kyiv died in a fire in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighborhood as a result of Wednesday's attack, Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said.
He had warned last week the capital should now be on a war footing as the enemy was "tearing Kyiv apart" with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.
The renewed attacks had triggered scheduled power cuts Tuesday, which plunged parts of Kyiv into darkness to ease the pressure on the battered grid.
A familiar rumbling sound of the generators, used to get through power cuts, filled the streets again, bringing back memories of the previous winter, when systematic Russian attacks regularly cut power and heating.
In the evening, Zelenskyy warned residents to monitor for air raid sirens, saying in his nightly address that "there is updated intelligence information regarding the preparation by the Russians of a massive strike."
Military monitoring channels also said they expected a large-scale Russian attack, combining cruise and ballistic missiles with fast-moving jet-powered drones.
Zelenskyy said the military was "ready to respond, to the extent that our defense systems allow."
The air force said in the morning that it intercepted five ballistic missiles, as well as 39 cruise missiles and over 100 drones.
Ukraine has been struggling to down the new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, as well as the ballistic missiles that are harder to intercept.
"The children were absolutely terrified. Whenever there's heavy shelling, we try to head underground," Daria Medvedeva, 36, told AFP.
Concern has mounted about rising civilian casualties on both sides, as Ukraine also steps up its long-range attacks on Russian targets that it says are vital to its war effort.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's "just responses" to Russian strikes saw it hit two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions, as well as the Black Sea.

articles.title: Thousands joining French school protests met with tear gas, arrests
articles.summary: Police fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools Tuesday as students, teachers and parents held their largest demonstration yet against staff shortages and dilapi...
articles.full_text:
Police fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools Tuesday as students, teachers and parents held their largest demonstration yet against staff shortages and dilapidated classrooms.
In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs marked with "The state has killed national education" and other messages, in largely peaceful rallies. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.
But in Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.
"There is such a gap between the elites and us," said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg.
The protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris, before spreading nationwide, presenting a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's cash-strapped government at a time when it faces strong economic headwinds.
The High School Students Union said more than half of France's high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online.
"We want more money for the national educational system so that high schools are renovated," said Roberta, another recent high-school graduate at a protest outside Paris' prestigious Henri IV school.
Schools were facing a list of problems from water leaks to rat infestations, she added.
The government has responded to the demonstrations with riot police.
Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.
France's Interior Ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said, without specifying the crimes.
At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu's office.
A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France Monday. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade.
"They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters," said Omar Slaouti, a high school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris.
"If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake," he added.
Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and Le Pen's National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests. LFI denies the accusation.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.
The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.
Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government's words were not enough. "That's all fine and dandy, but that's not what's going to change the daily lives of our children," she said.
Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult.
The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt pile, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push bond yields higher. The yield on France's 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.
The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right euro-skeptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring's election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.

articles.title: Venezuela's Maduro, wife to face new US charges over alleged torture
articles.summary: Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who were abducted by U.S. agents, are expected to face new criminal charges in the U.S. over the alleged torture of...
articles.full_text:
Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who were abducted by U.S. agents, are expected to face new criminal charges in the U.S. over the alleged torture of Americans detained in Venezuela, a U.S. official said Wednesday.
The new charges could come as soon as Thursday, according to the official, who was briefed on the investigation.
Maduro and Flores were captured by the U.S. military from their homes in Caracas on Jan. 3 and brought to New York to face drug trafficking charges. They have pleaded not guilty.
A spokesperson for the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's office, which brought the charges, declined to comment.
Lawyers for Maduro and Flores did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The possibility of new charges was first reported by CNN on Wednesday.
Details of the new charges, including the identities of the alleged torture victims, were not immediately available.
Maduro's 13 years in power in oil-rich Venezuela were marked by tensions with the United States. Washington said that several of its citizens were wrongfully detained in the South American country during his tenure.
Venezuela has been led since Maduro's capture by his former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has increased cooperation with the Trump administration.
